claims.text: The proposed framework integrates machine learning with CALPHAD-derived descriptors and first-principles DFT phonon-transport calculations.
The hybrid framework will accurately identify HEA compositions with exceptionally low lattice thermal conductivity.
Machine learning can efficiently screen large HEA compositional spaces for promising candidates.
CALPHAD-derived thermodynamic and compositional descriptors allow the model to capture global compositional effects and thermodynamic stability.
DFT-based HEA calculations can represent chemical disorder and calculate transport-related properties.
DFT force-constant calculations account for local lattice distortions and subtle bonding variations in the target HEAs.
Lattice distortion in HEAs can reduce phonon velocity and enhance phonon scattering, thereby lowering lattice thermal conductivity.
Increasing chemical or configurational disorder reduces phonon mean free path and suppresses lattice thermal conductivity.
Variations in local bonding environments critically enhance phonon scattering in the target HEAs.
The intended materials are single-phase, compositionally well-defined equiatomic or near-equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloys and derivatives with established baseline thermal conductivity.
Combining data-driven correlations with atomistic phonon-scattering calculations narrows prediction errors relative to traditional empirical rules.
The hybrid model can attribute reductions in phonon mean free path to specific lattice distortions and disorder.
Predicted HEA compositions will have measured lattice thermal conductivities 20–30% lower than values estimated by conventional empirical approaches.
Hybrid-model predictions will agree with measured lattice thermal conductivity within 10–20%.
The framework is primarily applicable to single-phase HEAs without phase separation or severe compositional inhomogeneity.
Prediction accuracy may diminish in multiphase materials or when extrinsic defects dominate thermal transport.
Machine-learning prediction accuracy is sensitive to limited or sparse training data.
Thermal conductivity can be benchmarked over 300–800 K using laser-flash analysis or TDTR.
A deviation greater than 20% between measured conductivity and the hybrid prediction would falsify the stated predictive-accuracy hypothesis.
Absence of the predicted enhanced-phonon-scattering signatures would also falsify the proposed mechanism.
